reconcile.connective: Older commentators read ‘the world seeth me no more’ as bounded by time — ending precisely when Christ returns for every eye to see.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells (Skeptics Annotated Bible) credits the Watch Tower Society for flagging this pair, since its ‘invisible return’ reading of John 14:19 clashes with ‘every eye shall see him.’

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Will Jesus's second coming be visible to all?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/seejesus.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Will Jesus's second coming be visible to all?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: The men of the world now see me with their bodily eyes, which is all the sight they have of me; and this they will be deprived of in a very little time; they will see me no more until the time that I shall come in the clouds of heaven to judge the world; and then every eye shall see me:
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly ties John 14:19's 'no more' to a time-limit ending at the parousia, when 'every eye' (the same phrase as Rev 1:7) will see him — the core reconcile move.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Those only that see Christ with an eye of faith shall see him for ever. The world sees him no more till his second coming; but his disciples have communion with him in his absence.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A second, independent voice stating the same temporal-bound harmonization outright ('till his second coming'), drawn from inside the anchored John 14 block.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on John 14:18-20 (1706-1714)
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats John 14:19's 'the world sees him no more' as bounded by time, ending at Christ's second coming — the same passage this row's reconcile pole draws from.
